subject: physics
title: Required practical: density
key_idea: To find a density, measure the mass and the volume, then divide. Find the volume of a regular solid from its dimensions and of an irregular solid by displacement. Repeat the readings and take a mean.

blocks.text: Every density method has two measurements: the mass and the volume. This section covers how to measure each one for a regular solid, an irregular solid and a liquid.

blocks.label: Density
where: density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³, or grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³
mass, m, in kilograms, kg, or grams, g
volume, V, in metres cubed, m³, or centimetres cubed, cm³

items: Mass: use a top pan balance for every solid.
Mass of a liquid: measure the mass of the empty container, then the container with the liquid, and subtract. Or zero the balance with the empty container on it.

blocks.label: Volume of a cuboid or cube
blocks.formula: volume = length × width × height    (V = l × w × h)
where: volume, V, in centimetres cubed, cm³
length, width and height, in centimetres, cm

items: Measure each dimension with a ruler, a micrometer or Vernier callipers.
A micrometer has a smaller resolution than a metre rule, so it gives a more accurate width.
Use a displacement method. The object pushes aside its own volume of water.
Measuring cylinder: volume of object = final volume − initial volume.
Displacement (eureka) can: fill the can to the spout, put the object in, collect the displaced water and measure its volume in a measuring cylinder.
For a very small object, add several identical objects together. Divide the change in volume by the number of objects.
Pour the liquid into a measuring cylinder.
Read the volume with your eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
Density = mass ÷ volume. Measure both.
Regular solid: calculate the volume from its dimensions. Irregular solid: use displacement.
Small objects: use several and divide the volume by the number.

blocks.text: This is the standard method for a rock or other irregular solid that sinks in water.

items.lead: Part fill a measuring cylinder with water.
Place the object in the water.

items.text: Volume of object = final volume − initial volume.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for finding the density of an irregular solid in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps for finding the density of an irregular solid in order.
steps: Measure the mass of the object with a balance
Part fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the initial volume
Place the object in the water and record the final volume
Subtract the initial volume from the final volume to find the volume of the object
Calculate the density using density = mass ÷ volume

diagram.alt: Calculate the density of an irregular solid from its mass and the water levels before and after.
diagram.question: A solid has a mass of {m} g. It is placed in a measuring cylinder containing 50 cm³ of water. The water level rises to {f} cm³. Calculate the density of the solid in g/cm³.
working: Volume of solid = final volume − initial volume = {f} − 50 cm³.

items: Mass first, then the volume by displacement, then divide.
The volume of the object is the change in water level, not the final reading.

blocks.text: Good results need careful reading and repeats. This section covers the main sources of error and how to reduce them.

items: Read a measuring cylinder with your eye level with the water, to avoid a parallax error.
In a displacement can, fill the water to the spout before the object goes in. Collect all of the displaced water.
Use equipment with a smaller resolution, such as a micrometer rather than a metre rule.
Use a balance that reads to more decimal places, and zero it with the empty container on it.
Use a larger volume of liquid, or a measuring cylinder with smaller divisions.
Repeat the measurements and calculate a mean. This reduces the effect of random errors and helps to identify anomalies.
Eye level with the scale, and the water level at the spout, reduce errors in the volume.
A smaller resolution means a more accurate measurement.
Repeating and finding a mean reduces the effect of random errors.

checks.q: Describe how to find the volume of a small stone using a measuring cylinder.
checks.a: Part fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the initial volume. Place the stone in the water and record the final volume. Volume of stone = final volume − initial volume.

checks.q: A student wants an accurate volume for one very small coin. How can displacement be used?
checks.a: Add several identical coins to the measuring cylinder. Measure the change in water level and divide by the number of coins.

checks.q: A rock has a mass of 90 g. The water level rises from 50 cm³ to 80 cm³ when it is added. Calculate the density.

exam_phrases: measure mass using a balance / scales
part fill a measuring cylinder with water and measure initial volume
volume of rock = final volume − initial volume
which reduces the effect of random errors
metre rule has a lower resolution
divide by the number of coins added

mistakes.wrong: The metre rule gives fewer decimal places, so it is less accurate.
mistakes.right: Fewer decimal places is not enough. Say the metre rule has a lower resolution, so it is less accurate than the micrometer.

mistakes.wrong: Measure one tiny coin in the measuring cylinder to find its volume.
mistakes.right: Add several coins and measure the change in water level. Then divide by the number of coins added.
Repeating allows a mean to be calculated. A mean reduces the effect of random errors, and anomalies can be identified.

worked_example.question: To help identify the type of rock, a student took measurements to determine its density. Describe a method the student could use to determine the density of the rock.
answer_points: measure the mass using a balance
part fill a measuring cylinder with water and measure the initial volume
place the rock in the water and measure the final volume
volume of rock = final volume − initial volume
use mass and volume to calculate the density
worked_example.tip: Marks are for a valid method with all key steps in a logical order. A displacement can with the displaced water collected in a measuring cylinder also scores.

exam_phrases: put marble(s) into water (in cylinder) and measure change in water level
ensure water measured at eye level

mistakes.wrong: Repeat the measurements and take an average, as the idea to improve accuracy.
mistakes.right: Repeating and averaging is ignored for that mark. Give a specific improvement, such as using several marbles or reading the water level at eye level.

mistakes.wrong: Density = 0.058 ÷ 6.5 = 0.0089 for a volume of 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ m³.
mistakes.right: Use the full volume: 0.058 ÷ (6.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 8.9 × 10³ kg/m³. Getting the power of ten wrong scores only 1 mark.

mistakes.wrong: Measure the volume of the copper by putting it in water and reading the final water level.
mistakes.right: Note the water level before and after, then find the difference. Or use a displacement can and collect the water from the spout.

worked_example.question: A student measures the density of glass. The student has a bag of marbles, all made from the same type of glass, a weighing balance and a plastic measuring cylinder containing water. Describe how the student could find, as accurately as possible, the density of the glass used for the marbles.
answer_points: find the mass of the marble(s) with the balance
put the marble(s) into the water and measure the change in water level
divide the mass by the volume (density = mass ÷ volume)
a suitable idea to improve accuracy, such as using several marbles, or reading the water at eye level
worked_example.tip: The fourth mark needs a specific improvement. Repeating and averaging is ignored.
